target.title: ZERO-SHOT PERSONALIZED LIP-TO-SPEECH SYNTHESIS WITH FACE IMAGE BASED VOICE CONTROL

read.pdf: Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Table 1, and Table 2 read from text.txt captions/transcriptions; separate PDF not present

entries.text: The authors claim the first zero-shot personalized Lip2Speech attempt that uses a face image rather than reference audio to control voice characteristics.
entries.condition: Authors' novelty claim; stated as best of their knowledge.
entries.quote: To our best knowledge, this paper makes the ﬁrst attempt on zero-shot personalized Lip2Speech synthesis with a face image rather than reference audio to control voice characteristics.

entries.text: The paper characterizes earlier multi-speaker methods as requiring target-speaker reference speech, which prevents voice control when only silent video of an unseen speaker is available.
entries.condition: Background claim about prior Lip2Speech methods at inference.

entries.text: A VAE is claimed to disentangle speaker identity from linguistic content so speaker embeddings can control unseen-speaker voice characteristics.
entries.condition: Method description; video-content posterior is KL-constrained toward a standard normal prior.
entries.quote: A variational autoencoder is adopted to disentangle the speaker identity and linguistic content representations, which enables speaker embeddings to control the voice characteristics of synthetic speech for unseen speakers.

entries.text: Associated cross-modal representation learning transfers speech-identity information to face-based speaker embeddings (FSE) for voice control.
entries.condition: Face encoder is trained with paired same-speaker face and speech using cosine-similarity, gender-contrastive, and face-classification losses.
entries.quote: Furthermore, we propose associated cross-modal representation learning to promote the ability of face-based speaker embeddings (FSE) on voice control.

entries.text: The authors claim their synthesized utterances are more natural and better match the input video's personality than the compared methods.
entries.condition: Authors' overall abstract-level comparison claim; experiments are on GRID.
entries.quote: whose synthetic utterances are more natural and matching with the personality of input video than the compared methods.

entries.text: At inference, face-encoder mode uses an unseen speaker's face image and does not require reference speech; the alternative speech-encoder mode requires a target-speaker reference utterance.
entries.condition: Face identity encoder selected for zero-shot mode; the first video frame supplies the face image.
entries.quote: When the face identity encoder is used, zero-shot personalized Lip2Speech synthesis can be achieved since no reference speech of unseen speakers is necessary any more.

entries.text: The video content encoder uses center-lip crops; the face identity encoder receives the first video frame for speaker identity.
entries.condition: GRID video input; 3D convolutional blocks, 2D ResNet-18, and two convolutional layers encode content.

entries.text: The video content encoder uses 3D convolutional blocks, a standard 2D ResNet-18, and two convolutional layers.
entries.condition: Lip-reading-style encoder architecture; input is synchronized talking-face video.

entries.text: GRID contains 33 speakers and 1K videos per speaker.
entries.condition: GRID corpus used for Lip2Speech experiments.

entries.text: Each GRID utterance contains six context-independent words in an artificially constrained recording environment.
entries.condition: GRID vocabulary and recording conditions; relevant to generalization claims.

entries.text: For the selected GRID seen speakers, utterances are split per speaker into training, development, and seen test subsets.
entries.condition: GRID main experiment; the selected-speaker counts and unseen-speaker test are recorded in separate entries.

entries.text: The speech identity encoder's pretraining corpus is VoxCeleb2, described as having over one million utterances from 6,112 celebrities.
entries.condition: External speech-identity pretraining; paper does not give VoxCeleb2 speaker split or overlap with GRID identities.

entries.text: VGGFace2 is described as around 3.31 million images in 9,131 identity classes for face-encoder pretraining.
entries.condition: External face-identity pretraining corpus.

entries.text: Cross-modal training used the 5,994 people shared by VoxCeleb2 and VGGFace2, pairing a random same-speaker face image and utterance.
entries.condition: External cross-modal representation learning; face and speech identity encoders are paired by person.

entries.text: GRID audio is resampled to 16 kHz and represented as 80-dimensional mel and 321-dimensional linear spectrograms.
entries.condition: Decoder ground-truth features for GRID Lip2Speech synthesis.

entries.text: The non-autoregressive Conformer decoder has five layers, each with 256-dimensional attention, four heads, and a 31×1 convolution kernel.
entries.value: 5 decoder layers; 256 attention dimensions; 4 heads; 31×1 kernel
entries.condition: GRID synthesis decoder configuration.

entries.text: The synthesis model is trained with Adam at learning rate 5e-4.
entries.condition: VAE-based Lip2Speech synthesis model; Adam optimizer.

entries.text: The face identity encoder is updated using cosine-similarity, gender-contrastive, and cross-entropy objectives.
entries.condition: Cross-modal face-encoder optimization; speech identity encoder is fixed.
entries.quote: the face identity encoder is updated by a cosine similarity lossLCS , a gender contrastive loss LGC and a cross-entropy lossLCE .

entries.text: Predicted linear spectrograms are phase-reconstructed with Griffin-Lim to produce synthesized waveforms.
entries.condition: No neural vocoder is described; the system uses Griffin-Lim after the post-net.
entries.quote: In the end, the Grifﬁn-Lim algorithm is used to recover phases from the linear spectrograms and to reconstruct the ﬁnal waveforms.

entries.text: Objective metrics are STOI, ESTOI, PESQ, and EER; lower EER is interpreted as greater speaker similarity.
entries.condition: Evaluation includes objective intelligibility/quality/speaker-similarity scores and subjective MOS-SN and MOS-FVM.
entries.quote: Lower EER indicates better similarity between the voice characteristics of the synthesized speech and that of the ground truth.

entries.text: Twenty sentences were randomly selected from the test set and synthesized by the five systems for subjective evaluation.
entries.condition: Amazon Mechanical Turk MOS-SN and MOS-FVM subjective evaluation.
entries.quote: 20 sentences were randomly selected from the test

entries.text: Twenty listeners scored each synthetic utterance on a 1–5 scale for naturalness and face-voice match.
entries.condition: Amazon Mechanical Turk; MOS-SN and MOS-FVM; the paper does not state rater demographics.
entries.quote: A total of 20 listeners participated in the test

entries.text: The authors report Proposed significantly outperforming Proposed-VAE on every metric for unseen speakers (paired t-tests, p<0.05), especially MOS-FVM.
entries.condition: Paired t-tests; unseen GRID speakers; Table 1 Proposed vs Proposed-VAE.
entries.quote: We can see that the Proposed system outperformed the Proposed-V AE system on all metrics signiﬁcantly (p <0.05 in paired t-tests) for unseen speakers, especially on MOS-FVM.

entries.text: For unseen speakers, the authors report Proposed significantly improves MOS-FVM and EER over Proposed-CML, attributing this to the three face-encoder losses.
entries.condition: Paired t-tests; unseen GRID speakers; Table 1 Proposed vs Proposed-CML.

entries.text: The authors regard Proposed Speech, which uses speech identity embeddings, as an upper-bound variant for face-based Proposed.
entries.condition: Authors' interpretation; Proposed Speech uses target-speaker reference utterances and is not zero-shot.

entries.text: The authors report VAE content representations are speaker-independent, whereas the no-VAE variant retains speaker information; synthesized-speech embeddings show gender separation for Proposed.
entries.condition: Qualitative t-SNE analysis on unseen speakers; the paper does not report a quantitative disentanglement score.
entries.quote: those in Proposed were speaker-independent.

entries.text: The authors concede a seen-speaker trade-off: Proposed has lower MOS-SN and three objective scores than Proposed-VAE, despite its better disentanglement.
entries.condition: Seen GRID speakers; comparison is between Proposed and Proposed-VAE.
entries.quote: indicating a trade-off between disentanglement and the speech quality of seen speakers.

entries.text: The authors' evaluation uses GRID's artificially constrained six-word utterances; they identify large-vocabulary performance as future work.
entries.condition: No large-vocabulary evaluation is reported.

entries.text: The authors claim the method is the first to jointly offer target-voice control and speech synthesis for unseen identities over the state of the art while retaining intelligibility.
entries.condition: Authors' novelty claim for multi-speaker video-to-speech; the paper's quantitative unseen-speaker protocol uses unseen input-video speakers and target voices seen in training.

entries.text: Adversarial speaker-classification losses are introduced to remove speaker identity from video embeddings and separate it from linguistic content.
entries.condition: Two paper variants are described: adversarial entropy maximization (dispel) and gradient reversal (rev. grad.).
entries.quote: To better disentangle the two inputs—linguistic content and speaker identity—we add adversarial losses that dispel the identity from the video embeddings.

entries.text: For SE, the frozen speaker-recognition network's 512-dimensional embeddings are projected to 32 dimensions by a learned linear layer.
entries.condition: SE uses utterance-level embeddings from the pretrained Xie et al. speaker-recognition network; linear projection is learned while that network is frozen.

entries.text: The quantitative control test pairs videos of unseen speakers with target voice identities of speakers seen during training.
entries.condition: GRID video-to-speech; unseen input-speaker videos and seen target voices; reported outputs are evaluated for content intelligibility and speaker identity.

entries.text: The EER protocol samples 20,000 natural/synthesized embedding pairs, including 1,460 positive same-speaker pairs and the remainder negative pairs.
entries.condition: Unseen video speakers paired with seen target voices; positive means synthesized and natural embeddings have the same speaker identity; negative means different identities; EER threshold varies cosine distance.

entries.text: The paper's naive random-distance EER chance benchmark is approximately 50%.

questions.q: Does the paper demonstrate face-only zero-shot voice control, and what does its comparison establish?
questions.answer: Yes, on held-out GRID speakers: Proposed uses the first-frame face embedding without unseen-speaker reference speech (t6, t25). On the unseen split it reports STOI 0.589, ESTOI 0.389, PESQ 1.454, EER 36.72, MOS-SN 2.817, and MOS-FVM 3.133 (t25). Ablations support the VAE and cross-modal losses, while the reference-speech Proposed Speech* comparison is a separate protocol and does not directly establish zero-shot superiority over prior systems (t26, t27, t32, t39).

questions.q: What is the strongest scope limitation on the evaluation?
questions.answer: The test is GRID, recorded in a constrained setting with six context-independent words per utterance; large-vocabulary performance is explicitly left for future work (t10, t38). The paper also does not disclose overlap between held-out GRID identities and external pretraining identities (t42).

The paper omits random seeds and run repetitions, exact objective-test counts/aggregation, checkpoint-selection criteria, feature/embedding normalization, EER backend/trials/unit convention, chance-level references, and the seen/unseen assignment of subjective samples; the number and duration of reference utterances are also unspecified for the reference-audio variant (t40–t48).

questions.q: What trade-off do the authors report for seen speakers?
questions.answer: They concede a seen-speaker quality trade-off: Proposed has lower MOS-SN and three objective scores than the no-VAE Proposed-VAE ablation, despite the reported disentanglement benefit (t37).

questions.q: Facetron (arXiv 2107.12003): where do speaker features come from at inference, how is the face encoder trained, is there an unseen-speaker test, with which metrics and values, and which waveform generator?
questions.answer: Face images through a FaceNet-based face encoder trained with a cosine-similarity loss to embeddings of a pre-trained (Mellotron) prosody encoder; GRID with 4 held-out speakers (s1, s2, s4, s29); unseen WER 14.7%, MOS 3.87, gender recognition 99.22% (speaker similarity not tested for unseen speakers); HiFi-GAN vocoder.
